Cleaned Description: The image is an architecture diagram depicting a Motion Guided Generation Network (MGGN) for joint feature and video compression. The diagram consists of two main components: the Sparse Point Prediction Network (SPPN) and the Motion Guided Generation Network (MGGN).||        The SPPN takes two input frames, \(I_t\) (target frame) and \(I_k\) (key frame), and predicts sparse motion patterns \(m_t\) and \(m_k\) for each frame. These motion patterns are then used to compute the difference heatmap \(\Delta \tilde{H}\).||        The MGGN comprises several modules:|        1. **Flow Estimator**: This module estimates the motion flow between the key frame \(I_k\) and the target frame \(I_t\) using the difference heatmap \(\Delta \tilde{H}\) and the appearance information from \(I_k\). The output is a flow map \(\xi_{k \rightarrow t}\).|        2. **Appearance Encoder**: This module encodes the appearance features of the key frame \(I_k\).|        3. **Deformation Module**: The encoded appearance features are deformed using the estimated flow map \(\xi_{k \rightarrow t}\) to align with the target frame.|        4. **Appearance Decoder**: This module decodes the deformed features and combines them with the difference heatmap \(\Delta \tilde{H}\) to generate the target frame \(\hat{I_t}\).||        The flow of information starts with the input frames \(I_t\) and \(I_k\) being processed by the SPPN to generate sparse motion patterns. These patterns are used to compute the difference heatmap, which, along with the key frame, is fed into the Flow Estimator to produce the flow map. The Appearance Encoder extracts features from the key frame, which are then deformed and decoded by the Appearance Decoder to generate the final target frame.|

These layers are also followed by BN, ReLU, and max-pooling.||        The fusion module combines the learned features from both networks. Three classifiers are constructed, and each CNN has an output layer. The fused features are also fed into an output layer. The fusion process involves both feature-level and decision-level fusions. Feature-level fusion methods include summation and maximization, while decision-level fusion uses a weighted summation method.||        The diagram illustrates the flow of information from the input modules through the feature learning modules, where weight sharing occurs, to the fusion module, which integrates the features and produces the final output.|

Cleaned Description: The image depicts the architecture of the Sparsemax Global Attention Feature (Sparsemax-GAF) network. The process begins with an input feature that undergoes three parallel 1x1 convolution operations. Each convolution output is then reshaped. One of the reshaped outputs is transposed and then combined with the other reshaped outputs through matrix multiplication. The resulting product is passed through a sparsemax layer to generate a sparsemax attention map. This attention map is then projected back onto the original input feature map using matrix multiplication to obtain the attended feature. The attended feature is then reshaped and combined with the shortcut input feature through elementwise summation to produce the final Global Attention Feature (GAF).|

Cleaned Description: The image is an architecture diagram depicting the RF-ReID model for person re-identification using RF signals. The process begins with an input RF tracklet, which is temporally sampled into RF segments of 3 seconds (90 frames). These segments are then processed by the RF Feature Extraction Network, which extracts frame-level features. The extracted features are then fed into a Multi-Headed Hierarchical Attention (MHA) module.||        The MHA module consists of two sub-modules: the first attention sub-module (dark blue) aggregates frame-level features to extract segment-level features, while the second attention sub-module (light blue) aggregates segment-level features to extract tracklet-level features. The supervision for training the RF feature extraction network and the first attention sub-module is applied to the segment-level features, and the supervision for the second attention sub-module is applied to the tracklet features.||        The RF feature extraction network uses spatio-temporal convolutions to extract global features from the input RF frames, followed by cropping the region of interest around the tracklet trajectory. The cropped features are then processed to generate frame-level identifiable features for person re-identification.||        The hierarchical attention module addresses the challenge of aggregating information across frames in the same tracklet due to the specularity of RF frames. The first attention block aggregates shape information within each 90-frame segment, while the second attention block aggregates walking style information across the entire tracklet.||        The model is trained using a multi-task learning approach, incorporating identification loss, triplet loss, and skeleton loss. The first attention layer is trained end-to-end with the feature extraction network, while the second attention layer is trained using the aggregated segment features. The final output is a tracklet feature that can be used for person re-identification.|

The framework consists of four main modules:||        (a) Image Patch Generation: This module starts with non-standard DICOM images from which image patches are generated. These patches are checked for soft tissue content. If soft tissue is present, the patches are categorized as soft tissue image patches. If the patches are overlapped, they are further processed as overlapped soft tissue image patches.||        (b) Standard Image Patch Synthesis: In this module, the soft tissue image patches are used to synthesize new image patches using the STAN-CT generator (G). Qualified synthesized image patches are stored, while unqualified ones are discarded.||        (c) Standard DICOM Image Generation: This module involves normalizing the image patches and integrating them using soft tissue masks. High-quality images are stored as qualified synthesized DICOM images.||        (d) DICOM Image Evaluation: The final module involves comparing the synthesized DICOM images with the original non-standard DICOM images. Radiologists evaluate these images side-by-side using a PACS reading workstation. Their reports, along with automatic performance evaluation based on image texture features, are used to generate standardized DICOM images with quality control (QC) reports.||        The flow of information across these modules ensures that the output DICOM images are standardized and of high quality, suitable for clinical use.|
